title: Serving Runtime — Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Benchmarking Playbook (Consolidated)
author: Ava Mitchell
summary: Consolidated reference for Redwood's serving runtime covering architecture, kernel scheduling strategy, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, release notes, known issues, operational runbooks and team wiki navigation. Intended as the single-entry guide for engineers and SREs responsible for runtime performance and reliability.
body:
Overview

This document consolidates our canonical guidance for the serving runtime used across Hosted, Dedicated and Private deployments. It is aimed at runtime engineers, perf engineers, SREs and on-call responders. Sections include: architecture overview, kernel scheduling design and policies, profiling playbook (how-to), benchmarking suite and workflows, recent release notes, known issues and operational runbooks.

1) Runtime architecture — high level

The serving runtime is composed of the following logical subsystems:
- Frontend router: request admission, authentication, routing by policy (latency / cost / region).
- Dispatcher: per-model dispatch queues, admission control, and per-tenant SLAs.
- Execution engine: GPU-optimized inference engine implementing attention kernels, KV cache management, quantized execution paths, and streaming output.
- Batcher: continuous batching subsystem that coalesces compatible requests into micro-batches.
- Cache layer: prefix/KV cache with adaptive eviction (LRU + frequency heuristics) and cross-request reuse.
- Telemetry & tracing: per-token metrics, per-request trace ids, sample-based traces forwarded to observability backend (Tracing service).
- Control plane: model catalog, versioning, rollout (canary/A-B), config store and autoscaling policies.

Design goals: deterministic tail latency (p99 SLOs), cost-efficiency (batching + quantization), graceful degradation (model fallbacks), and operational observability.

Architecture diagram (text)
- Clients -> Frontend Router -> Dispatcher -> Batcher -> GPU Execution Engine -> KV Cache / External storage (S3)
- Control plane interacts with Dispatcher for rollout config and with Execution Engine for kernel/quantization profiles.

2) Kernel scheduling — strategy and policies

We use a hybrid scheduling model: static kernel selection at model load time combined with dynamic scheduling based on observed seq_len distributions and queue pressure. Key policies:
- Kernel selection: when a model is onboarded a kernel profile is generated for common sequence-length buckets (<=128, 129-512, 513-2048, >2048). The control plane pins preferred kernels per bucket.
- Work-stealing micro-scheduler: each GPU worker maintains local queues per sequence bucket; a low-latency work-stealer pulls from adjacent queues to avoid head-of-line blocking.
- Latency-sensitive fast-path: requests tagged with latency=SLO are prioritized into a fast-path queue (strict preemption within a micro-batch window).
- Cost-optimized slow-path: background requests (batchable, non-SLO) are aggregated into larger batches and scheduled during low load.
- Kernel prewarming: hot kernels are prewarmed based on rolling 15-minute usage windows and de-warmed after 30 minutes of inactivity.

Kernel tuning knobs (config table)
| config_key | description | default | operator impact |
|---|---|---:|---|
| kernel_profile_buckets | sequence length buckets used for kernel selection | "[128,512,2048]" | changing splits affects latency/cost tradeoffs |
| prewarm_threshold | calls/min to mark kernel hot | "10" | lower value increases GPU memory footprint |
| fast_path_share | fraction of HW slots reserved for fast-path | "0.15" | raising reduces throughput for background jobs |

3) Profiling playbook — step-by-step

Purpose: collect reproducible profiles for performance regressions, p99 tail events, and kernel inefficiencies.
Pre-req: SSH access to perf cluster (team: serving-runtime), access to profiling bucket and perf-runner tooling.

Steps:
1. Reproduce at scale: use perf-runner to replay representative traffic (use exact model version and prompt distribution). Command example: perf-runner --scenario=chat-mixed --rate=500rps --duration=15m --model=redwood-gpt-13b-q4_0
2. Collect traces: enable distributed tracing sample rate to 100% for the run (temporary).
3. Capture GPU telemetry: run nvprof/nv-smi sampling on the target worker nodes (10s sampling window every minute). Save to profiling bucket: s3://redwood-perf/profiles/<run-id>/
4. Kernel-level traces: enable our kernel tracer (ktrace) for the execution engine: /opt/redwood/bin/ktrace --out /tmp/ktrace-<run-id>.log --pid <exec-agent>
5. Aggregate and visualize: run perf-agg to consolidate CPU/GPU/trace timelines and upload to perf-dashboard.
6. Analysis checklist: 
   - check queue occupancy vs latency spikes
   - identify kernels with high SM utilization but low achieved throughput (kernel stalls)
   - verify KV cache hit ratios and their relation to prefix reuse
   - inspect batch size distribution and per-batch variance
7. Mitigation steps: follow the prioritization table in the mitigation section (hot kernel tuning, adjusting prewarm thresholds, increasing fast-path share, or temporary capacity scale-up).

4) Benchmarking suite — reproducible workflows

We maintain a canonical benchmarking harness (bench-suite) with workloads: chat-mix, completion-heavy, embedding-throughput, and rerank. Benchmarks are versioned in the repo infra/benchmarks and are executed nightly and on release gates.

Benchmark procedure:
- Baseline: run bench-suite on hermetic cluster (controlled background load = 0) to get single-GPU throughput and p50/p95/p99.
- Stress: run at target QPS for 30 minutes to measure sustained throughput and failure modes.
- Regression check: compare against last known good baseline; automatically create an issue if p95 or cost/unit regresses by >5% or p99 regresses by >10%.

Artifacts produced: CSV of latency vs batch size, kernel utilization heatmaps, cost-per-token estimations (based on current pricing model), and a benchmark summary.md. Artifacts are stored at s3://redwood-bench/<date>/<model-version>/

5) Release notes (latest: 2029-12-12)

Version: runtime-2029.12.12
Highlights:
- Improved kernel prewarming algorithm to reduce cold start p99 by 18% for seq_len <=512 workloads.
- Added new micro-scheduler heuristic to prefer contiguous sequence-length grouping, reducing wasted padding and improving throughput by ~7% for heterogeneous workloads.
- Introduced per-tenant fast_path_share override (controlled via model config).
- Resolved memory leak in KV cache eviction logic (issue #SR-8421).

Upgrade notes:
- Rolling deploy is supported; priority customers (Dedicated) will be scheduled to opt-in for the first canary wave.
- If you operate private deployments: new control-plane flag kernel_profile_buckets must be applied prior to rolling agents. See migration steps in related_pages.

6) Known issues (operational)

- SR-9012: Intermittent p99 spikes for long-context (>2048) streaming requests when run on T4-like hardware. Mitigation: route long-context requests to the high-memory pool or reduce micro-batch size for >2048 bucket. Status: mitigated in 2029.12.12 for A100 fleets; T4 mitigation recommended.
- SR-8421: KV cache eviction race causing temporary OOM on heavy churn workloads. Fix applied in 2029.12.12; backport pending for older branches.
- SR-9120: perf-runner on macOS clients may fail when TLS cipher set is restricted. Workaround: use linux runner container.

7) Runtime runbooks — quick operational playbooks

P1: p99 tail spike (serving-runtime)
1. Triage: check dashboards (per-route p99, per-model batch size distribution, kernel hotness) -> dashboards/serving/runtime-overview.
2. Identify root cause: run the quick profiler: /opt/redwood/bin/quickprof --model <id> --duration 120s 
3. Short-term mitigations (choose one):
   - increase fast_path_share to 0.3 for impacted route
   - scale up worker pool by +20% (if autoscaler is not reactive)
   - apply temporary routing rule to use a lower-seq model variant
4. Post-incident: run full profiling playbook and open a perf investigation ticket.

P2: GPU OOM on worker node
1. Alert arrives -> ssh to node; check dmesg and docker logs for OOM kill.
2. If OOM due to KV cache: clear cache for tenant: curl -X POST $CONTROL_PLANE/cache/clear?tenant=<tenant_id>
3. If OOM due to stuck process: restart exec-agent: systemctl restart redwood-exec-agent && monitor.
4. If recurring: drain node and run heap/profile capture.
